post.caption: Rhinestones are named for the Rhine River. It translates the French caillou du Rhin, meaning Rhine pebble. The first ones were said to be rock crystal from the Rhine. Clear rock crystal was a cheap way to imitate diamond. Today rhinestones are usually glass or paste. Georg Friedrich Strass, an Alsatian jeweler, worked in Paris around 1730. He coated the underside of lead glass with metal powder. Strass still means rhinestone in many European languages. Daniel Swarovski patented an electric machine for cutting crystal in 1892. He founded his firm in Wattens, Austria, in 1895.
